q-290907.worked_solution:
We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}1.40 & 1.37 & -0.49 \\ 0.59 & 0.29 & -0.70 \\ -0.97 & -1.18 & -0.66 \\ -0.15 & 0.27 & 1.67 \\ -0.86 & -0.75 & 0.18\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.713 & 0.123 & -0.47 & 0.506 & 0.013 \\ -0.25 & 0.321 & 0.709 & 0.213 & 0.535 \\ 0.509 & 0.422 & 0.046 & 0.667 & -0.342 \\ 0.042 & -0.839 & 0.241 & 0.487 & 0.01 \\ 0.41 & -0.027 & -0.465 & 0.133 & 0.773\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.809 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2.020 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.114 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}-0.711 & 0.051 & 0.701 \\ -0.693 & -0.218 & -0.687 \\ 0.118 & -0.975 & 0.191\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{2.809}^{2}}{{2.809}^{2}+{2.020}^{2}+{0.114}^{2}}≈65.8%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{2.809}^{2}+{2.020}^{2}}{{2.809}^{2}+{2.020}^{2}+{0.114}^{2}}≈99.9%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $65.8%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $99.9%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

EXPLANATION

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is the direction in feature space with the most variance.

The second principal component is the direction orthogonal to the first principal component.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to standardize the data.

The standardized data matrix is

Xstd=[1.401.37−0.490.590.29−0.70−0.97−1.18−0.66−0.150.271.67−0.86−0.750.18].

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[−0.7130.123−0.470.5060.013−0.250.3210.7090.2130.5350.5090.4220.0460.667−0.3420.042−0.8390.2410.4870.010.41−0.027−0.4650.1330.773],Σ=[2.8090002.0200000.114000000],V=[−0.7110.0510.701−0.693−0.218−0.6870.118−0.9750.191].

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 2.80922.8092+2.0202+0.1142≈65.8%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 2.8092+2.02022.8092+2.0202+0.1142≈99.9%.

Thus, we have that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 65.8% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 99.9% of the variance.

If we wish to preserve 90% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

Writing v1,v2,v3 for the columns of V and u1,u2,u3,u4,u5 for the columns of U, the reduced dataset is

Xred=Xstd⋅[v1v2], since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of V.

Note: In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset X. Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

q-355845.worked_solution:
In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=3.171,\,{\sigma }_{2}=1.32,\,{\sigma }_{3}=0.477.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.171}^{2}}{{3.171}^{2}+{1.32}^{2}+{0.477}^{2}}≈83.6%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.171}^{2}+{1.32}^{2}}{{3.171}^{2}+{1.32}^{2}+{0.477}^{2}}≈98.1%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $83.6%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $98.1%$ of the variance.

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions},$ since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $95%$ of the variance.

EXPLANATION

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is the direction in feature space with the most variance.

The second principal component is the direction orthogonal to the first principal component.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to standardize the data.

The standardized data matrix is

Xstd=[−0.810.250.140.060.38−0.160.12−0.84−1.25−0.94−1.13−0.251.571.341.53].

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[−0.0660.590−0.424−0.0670.6800.055−0.056−0.5050.841−0.178−0.374−0.731−0.0630.0570.565−0.4300.3170.6750.4870.1520.817−0.1160.3250.2200.405],Σ=[3.1240001.3090000.738000000],V=[0.544−0.8020.2480.6080.173−0.7750.5780.5720.581].

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 3.12423.1242+1.3092+0.7382≈81.2%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 3.1242+1.30923.1242+1.3092+0.7382≈95.5%.

Thus, we have that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 81.2% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 95.5% of the variance.

If we wish to preserve 90% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

Writing v1,v2,v3 for the columns of V and u1,u2,u3,u4,u5 for the columns of U, the reduced dataset is

Xred=Xstd⋅[v1v2], since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of V.

Note: In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset X. Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.
